qs.q: Which member of the paramyxovirus family can cause very serious croup?
qs.e: RSV is the leading cause of severe croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) and bronchiolitis in infants and young children, causing subglottic swelling that produces the classic barking seal cough and inspiratory stridor.

es.q: A 4-year-old child presents with a harsh, persistent cough and inspiratory stridor. Based on the common causes of laryngotracheobronchitis (croup), identify the most common viral pathogen responsible for this condition in children.
es.m: The most common cause of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) in children is the parainfluenza virus.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A child presents with acute onset of inspiratory stridor and a harsh persistent cough, characteristic of Croup. What is the most common viral cause of Croup, and what is the primary bacterial causative agent for Acute Epiglottitis?
es.m: The most common cause of Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis) is the parainfluenza virus, typically affecting children. The primary causative agent for Acute Epiglottitis, predominantly in children, is *H. influenzae*.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Croup is viral laryngotracheobronchitis causing a barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor in young children. Diagnosis is clinical, severity is staged by stridor and retractions.

sections.p: Croup is an acute inflammation of the larynx, trachea and main bronchi, most often viral. Diagnosis is clinical: barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor after a recent upper‑respiratory infection.
b: No imaging needed unless atypical presentation
Chest X‑ray may show steeple sign but is not required

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Westley croup score (stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, consciousness). Mild: occasional bark, no stridor at rest. Moderate: frequent bark, audible stridor at rest, mild retractions. Severe: marked stridor, severe retractions, agitation or cyanosis.

Most cases are viral, especially parainfluenza type 1. Other viruses include RSV, influenza, adenovirus, and measles. In low‑resource settings consider co‑infection with HIV or TB that can worsen airway inflammation.
Child aged 6 months‑3 years develops a dry, barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, often worsening at night. Fever is low‑grade; breathing may be rapid with chest wall retractions.
Investigations are limited; they are used to rule out mimics or complications.

t.b: Is oxygenation adequate? Low SpO2 (<92%) signals severe disease needing supplemental O₂
Is there subglottic narrowing (steeple sign)? Helpful when diagnosis is unclear; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture
Is there leukocytosis suggesting bacterial superinfection? Mild elevation is common; marked rise may prompt antibiotics

sections.p: Rapid deterioration, severe retractions, cyanosis, lethargy, or inability to drink indicate impending airway obstruction. Complications include bacterial tracheitis and secondary pneumonia.
Treat inflammation, maintain airway patency and give supportive care. Nebulised epinephrine for moderate‑severe cases, oral dexamethasone for all severities, humidified air is optional.
b: Nebulised epinephrine – rapid bronchodilation for airway edema
Oral dexamethasone – reduces inflammation for 12‑24 h
Avoid routine antibiotics unless bacterial superinfection is evident

sections.p: Observe for at least 2‑4 hours after epinephrine; discharge if stable. Educate caregivers on signs of worsening. Vaccination against influenza and measles reduces viral triggers.
b: Re‑assessment within 2 h after nebulised epinephrine

sections.p: Conditions that cause stridor or cough in children.
b: Epiglottitis – high fever, drooling, muffled voice
Bacterial tracheitis – toxic appearance, purulent secretions

sections.p: Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude croup; mild leukocytosis is common and may be misinterpreted as bacterial infection.
b: Steeple sign absent in up to 30 % of cases

faq.q: Why is dexamethasone preferred over other steroids?
faq.a: It has a long half‑life, works orally, and reduces airway edema without needing repeat dosing.
For moderate to severe croup with audible stridor at rest or significant retractions.
It may provide comfort but does not alter disease course; evidence does not support routine use.
